compulsory

kum-PUL-suh-ree — stress the PUL; a compulsory rule pulls you in whether you like it or not. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Compulsory is required by a law, rule, or authority, leaving no choice about whether to do it.

Wearing a seatbelt is compulsory in nearly every state, no matter how short the drive.

Example

A school announces that attendance at the fire drill is compulsory for every student and staff member, with no exceptions for any reason. Anyone who skips it faces a serious penalty.

The rule allows absolutely no exceptions and carries a real penalty for skipping it. Unlike 'recommended,' which merely suggests, compulsory means there is no legal choice in the matter.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

mandatory: Mandatory means a rule or law does the requiring — mandatory training, mandatory reporting. It is compulsory's closest twin, and in most sentences the two trade places freely; compulsory leans slightly more formal and more toward what a government imposes on everyone, as in compulsory education or compulsory military service.

obligatory: Obligatory means required as a duty or by rule, and it stretches to social expectation — the obligatory thank-you note, the obligatory group photo — where no law is anywhere in sight. Compulsory keeps its legal teeth: an authority requires it, and skipping it carries a real penalty.

required: Required is the plain umbrella word: anything a rule, a need, or a situation demands is required, from passport photos to required reading. Compulsory sits at the strong end of that scale — the demand comes from a law or authority with the power to punish, so opting out is not open to you.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

optional: available to choose or not choose

voluntary: done by free choice, not forced

Where it sits · how impossible it is to skip — recommended → compulsory → unavoidable

recommended vs. compulsory: A recommended action is only advised — you can skip it without punishment — while a compulsory one comes with real consequences for skipping it.

unavoidable vs. compulsory: Unavoidable is stronger than compulsory: a compulsory rule is imposed by an authority, but something unavoidable cannot be escaped no matter what anyone decides.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — com-

prefix — com-: together, intensive (Latin)

root — -puls-

root — -puls-: to drive, to push (Latin)

suffix — -ory

suffix — -ory: relating to (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin compellere meant 'to drive together, to force.' Something compulsory is imposed with force — you are driven or pushed to do it, with no real choice.

Use the root in a new word: propel

Use the root in a new word: propel: The wind was strong enough to propel the small sailboat across the bay.
